# A0 · See it update ---------------------------------------------------------
# A ready count plot of one of your Fairness columns. Nothing to code.
# YOUR TURN (kickoff): change one word in the title, then render the report

Part A · Fairness

A0 · See it update

a0_column <- pick_a_column(fairness)

a0 <- ggplot(fairness, aes(y = .data[[a0_column]])) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "My Adult Workclass Plot", x = "Count", y = a0_column)

show_plot(a0)

Yes; both updated

A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = sex,
    has_outcome = (income == ">50K")
  )

a1_base <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Shares of people with an income over 50K/yr",
    subtitle = "Divided by sex",
    x = "Percent with income >50K/yr",
    y = "Sex",
    fill = "Income >50k/yr?"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

show_plot(a1)

The legend label is the most valuable change; the outcome was not originally listed, and therefore could not be interpreted without access to source code.

A2 · Choose a scale

a2 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
a2 <- fairness %>%
  filter(age > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribition of our findings based on age", x = "Age (Years, log scale)", y = "Count")

# YOUR TURN: one sentence. Why this scale for this column?
a2_reason <- "Ages are skewed roughly, and we can see which ages have a central majority contribution."

show_plot(a2)

With the log10scale, readers are more clearly able to see the pattern of what ages are most common in the dataset; no values were removed, but now our graph has a far greater shape.

A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

# YOUR TURN 1: replace "replace me" with your second column (no quotes).
a3_rates <- a_data %>%
  mutate(panel = sex) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = mean(has_outcome), .groups = "drop")

a3_fixed <- NULL
a3_free <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
   geom_col() +
   facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
   scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
   labs(title = "Percentage of people with income >50K per sex", x = "Sex", y = "Percentage of all data (%)")
a3_free <- a3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "Fixed allows for proportions to be compared far more easily."

show_plot(a3_fixed)
show_plot(a3_free)

The Fixed axis is most accurate. While the free y-axis graph does show the correct markings per graph, it misleads the reader to believe the rate of males and the rate of females with the outcome of 50K or above is near-even. The females panel is roughly half the count of the males panel, at 1657 compared to 3343, and therefore even a minor change in interpretation could be incorrect.

A4 · Compared to what?

a4_clouds <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 1: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___: the column
# with your groups, two of its values, and your numeric column.
a4_clouds <- a_data %>%
  filter(marital_status %in% c("Never-married", "Married-civ-spouse")) %>%
  make_clouds(marital_status, hours_per_week)

a4 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
a4 <- ggplot(a4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(title = "Hours worked per week for those married vs never married", x = "Marital Status", y = "Hours/week (units)")

show_plot(a4)

Individual values overlap very frequently, and have similar spread; however, the means show that those who are traditionally married work, on average, more hours per week than those who have never been married.

A5 · Color for every reader

a5 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___ (the same
# column in both places, so its name is on the axis too).
a5 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = marital_status, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(vars(sex)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Marital status of each observation distributed by sex", x = "Count", y = "Marital Status", fill = "Sex")

show_plot(a5)
# See it: your plot as a reader with red-green color blindness might see it.
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(a5)
2 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 99.5 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                  119.  Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                81.3 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = factor(rounds),
    has_outcome = agreement == 'Agree',
    value = abs(judge1_margin)
  )

b1_base <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "MMA Matches",
    subtitle = "Agreement outcome proportions based on rounds per match",
    x = "Proportions",
    y = "Rounds/match"
  )

show_plot(b1)

WRITE (2 sentences): What does the plot show? Which label helps a reader most?

B2 · Choose a scale

b2 <- b_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = after_stat(count / sum(count)))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Distribition of our findings based on age", x = "Age (Years, log scale)", y = "Count")


b2_reason <- "Shares displays what percentage of matches fall where the absolute judge1_margin is in each number within the small scale"

show_plot(b2)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Which scale, and why? If values were removed, say how many.

B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_rates <- b_data %>%
  mutate(panel = rounds) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = mean(has_outcome), .groups = "drop")

b3_fixed <- ggplot(b3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Percentage of matches with outcome by number of rounds", x = "Number of Rounds", y = "Percentage w/ Agreement")
b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")


b3_choice <- "fixed"
b3_reason <- "It is, once again, far easier to comprehend the distribution when a set y-scale is in place."

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)

WRITE (3–4 sentences): Fixed or free? What does the reader gain, and what do they lose? Which panels are small, and what is their n? Differences, not causes.

B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  filter(result_type %in% c("Unanimous", "Split")) %>%
  make_clouds(result_type, abs(judge1_margin))
b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(title = "Judge1 Margin with Split and Unanimous match results", x = "Judge1 Margin", y = "Result Type")


show_plot(b4)

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Do the clouds overlap? What does that say about individuals versus the group means?

B5 · Color for every reader

b5 <- b_data %>% mutate(agreement = if_else(agreement %in% c("judge1", "judge2", "judge3"), "judge", agreement)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = factor(rounds), fill = agreement)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(vars(agreement)) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Number of matches per agreement value by matches in a round", y = "Rounds/match", x = "Matches Count (scaled by log10)", fill = "Agreement Value")

show_plot(b5)
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(b5)
